sections.skill: Identify the conclusion, premises and assumptions of an argument

questions.prompt: What is the conclusion of an argument?

choices.text: The final sentence of any paragraph, whatever that sentence happens to say or do

questions.intro: An ARGUMENT gives reasons for a claim. The CONCLUSION is the claim being argued for. PREMISES are the reasons given. ASSUMPTIONS are unstated beliefs the argument needs. Example: "AI tutors answer questions instantly. Instant answers help students learn. So schools should use AI tutors." Conclusion: schools should use AI tutors. Premises: AI tutors answer instantly; instant answers help learning. Assumption: the answers are accurate and students still think for themselves. To evaluate an argument, ask whether the premises are true and whether they really support the conclusion.

sections.skill: Label the parts of an argument

questions.prompt: Which word often signals a conclusion?

choices.text: "Because," which usually comes right before the main claim that is being argued for

questions.intro: Find the parts in order. (1) Find the CONCLUSION: look for "so," "therefore," "should." (2) Find the PREMISES: the reasons, often after "because" or "since." (3) Ask what must ALSO be true for the reasons to support the conclusion: that is an ASSUMPTION. Example: "Since AI can write code, coding classes are useless." Conclusion: coding classes are useless. Premise: AI can write code. Assumption: if AI can do something, people need not learn it.

questions.prompt: "Some chatbots invented sources, so all AI answers are made up." What is the weak spot?
questions.intro: Common weak spots include: a premise stated as fact without evidence; a jump from "some" to "all"; ignoring other explanations; and loaded words that assume the conclusion ("obviously dangerous"). You can disagree with a conclusion and still find an argument well built, or agree with a conclusion and find the argument weak. Separating the parts helps you discuss AI questions calmly and precisely.
